translation:
  text: 'I saw six tall, glorious men arrive, alike in appearance. They called a crowd of men. Those who
    came were tall, handsome and strong. The six men ordered them to build a tower on top of the rock.[a]
    The men who had come to build the tower made a great commotion, running here and there around the
    gate.


    2. The virgins standing around the gate told the men to hurry with the building of the tower. They
    stretched out their hands as if about to receive something from the men.


    3. The six men ordered stones to rise from a certain depth and go into the building of the tower.
    Ten square, bright stones came up, which had not been cut.[b]


    4. The six men called the virgins and ordered them to carry all the stones intended for the building
    of the tower, pass through the gate, and hand them to the men who were going to build the tower.


    5. The virgins loaded one another with the first ten stones that had risen from the depth, carrying
    them together, one stone at a time.[c]'
  philosophy: optimal-equivalence
  footnotes:
  - marker: a
    reason: textual_variant
    text: '“On top of the rock” follows the previously recorded bounded Athos selection. The 1891 working
      body conjectures gate; its apparatus reports Vulgata gate, Palatina both rock and gate, and Ethiopic
      rock. Hilgenfeld (1873), p. 118 prints rock as an emendation while reporting gate in its Latin manuscripts;
      printed Latin rock is not an independent manuscript vote. Michigan’s decisive noun is lost. Alternatives:
      “build a tower on top of the gate”; “build a tower on top of the rock and above the gate.”'
  - marker: b
    reason: textual_variant
    text: '“Not” is bracketed in the working Greek: Anger’s insertion, absent from Athos, Vulgata and
      Ethiopic as reported; Palatina omits the cutting adjective too. Hilgenfeld (1873), p. 118 prints
      bracketed non and explicitly says it was supplied, not read in its manuscripts. Palatina (1877),
      p. 203 has bright square stones without a cutting adjective. Michigan loses a leaf before the disputed
      words, so cannot decide them. The draft provisionally retains the conjectural negative because S.
      9.v.3 explicitly describes the earlier stones as uncut. Alternatives: “Ten square, bright stones
      came up, which had been cut”; “Ten square, bright stones came up.” The parallel is internal evidence,
      not another manuscript witness.'
  - marker: c
    reason: textual_variant
    text: “Loaded one another” follows the printed conjecture epitithoun, compared with Palatina’s placing
      on one another; the reported Athos verb is disturbed. The women share each stone’s load, elaborated
      by the next paragraph’s corners and sides. The draft does not describe stacking the ten stones into
      a pile. Michigan’s missing leaf covers this clause and cannot certify the repaired verb.
